paragraphs: This paper studies regression as a competition between two predictors. Each player earns credit for the proportion of examples on which its prediction is closer to the correct value than its opponent’s prediction. This changes the learning objective: success depends on winning individual comparisons against another predictor, rather than simply pursuing accuracy without reference to a competitor.

The authors adapt the probably approximately correct learning framework to this prediction duel. They then develop an algorithm that finds a linear predictor serving as a best response to an opponent whose predictor need not be linear. The algorithm has linearithmic sample complexity, and its running time is polynomial when the input dimension is fixed.

Experiments also examine a high-dimensional setting, where the approach significantly beats classical regression algorithms under the duel’s scoring rule. These results support the usefulness of explicitly modeling competition in prediction tasks. The theoretical efficiency statement retains its fixed-dimension condition, while the experimental finding concerns competitive wins under the proposed payoff.
neurips-2017-best-response-regression-4f.tldr: The paper develops a theoretically grounded regression algorithm that competes by predicting more accurately than a given opponent on as many examples as possible.

paragraphs: This paper introduces convolutional structure into Gaussian processes to make them better suited to inputs such as images. Its goal is to combine the generalization benefits of a convolutional kernel with practical probabilistic inference. The central challenge is making that structured model computationally usable while retaining accurate estimates of its posterior.

The main contribution is an inter-domain inducing point approximation designed specifically for the convolutional kernel. This supplies an efficient approximation tailored to the model’s structure. The authors investigate several convolutional kernel variants and evaluate them on MNIST and CIFAR-10, reporting significant improvements over existing Gaussian process models.

The paper also uses marginal likelihood to select a weighting between convolutional and RBF kernels, which further improves performance. This gives a concrete example of using the model’s probabilistic objective to choose how different structural assumptions are combined. The authors suggest that this capability may help automate architecture discovery in larger models; that broader possibility is distinct from the demonstrated kernel-weighting result.
neurips-2017-convolutional-gaussian-proc.tldr: A tailored inference approximation makes convolutional Gaussian processes practical and improves image-task performance over existing Gaussian process models.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a machine learning model can contain a layer that solves a discrete optimization problem. A graph’s minimum cut is one motivating example. Such a layer poses a training difficulty because its output can change discontinuously, whereas end-to-end learning typically relies on gradients that describe how outputs respond to small parameter changes.

The authors establish an approach for submodular minimization layers. Their central idea is to replace the discrete output with a continuous relaxation while preserving guarantees. They also provide an approximation to the Jacobian that is easy to compute, together with a theoretical analysis. The Jacobian captures how the layer’s output responds to changes in its inputs or parameters.

These ingredients allow the authors to experimentally learn probabilistic log-supermodular models through a bi-level variational inference formulation. The contribution connects a structured optimization procedure to gradient-based learning: optimization becomes part of the trained model. The result is specifically developed for submodular minimization, rather than asserting that every discrete optimization algorithm can be incorporated this way.
neurips-2017-differentiable-learning-of-.tldr: Continuous relaxations and tractable derivative approximations enable submodular minimization layers to participate in gradient-based learning.

paragraphs: DPSCREEN constructs screening schedules that respond to both a patient’s characteristics and their evolving history. The decision is when to screen again, balancing frequent testing against delays in detecting disease. The framework also accounts for information outside scheduled appointments, such as self-examinations or newly discovered conditions, that can bring a patient to a clinician earlier.

The disease model is a finite-state stochastic process with an absorbing disease state: once that modeled state is reached, the process does not leave it. The clinician uses test results and external information to schedule the next visit. Because computing the exact optimal screening policy is computationally intractable, the paper develops a tractable construction of an approximately optimal policy.

An illustration using a large breast cancer dataset produces schedules that vary with initial risk and previous screening results. Compared with existing clinical policies, the constructed policy reduces the number of screens by 28–68% while maintaining the same expected detection delays. This finding concerns the policy comparison in that illustration and expresses a trade-off between screening frequency and expected detection timing.
neurips-2017-dpscreen-dynamic-personaliz.tldr: DPSCREEN builds approximately optimal personalized screening schedules, reducing screens in a breast cancer illustration while preserving expected detection delays.

paragraphs: This paper addresses estimation of the partition function, a key inference quantity in graphical models. It seeks an anytime method: the computation should provide useful estimates and bounds as it runs, with quality improving as more resources become available. The approach combines heuristic search, variational bounds, and Monte Carlo sampling within one dynamic importance sampling scheme.

Sampling uses a proposal defined through a variational method, while search progressively refines that proposal. An intelligently weighted average of the resulting samples gives an unbiased partition-function estimator with finite-sample confidence intervals. This weighting is central to obtaining the stated statistical properties while combining samples within the evolving procedure.

The resulting method brings together sampling’s rapid early improvement and the longer-term benefits of search improving the proposal. The authors report significantly better anytime behavior and greater flexibility in trading memory and computation time against solution quality. Experiments on real-world instances from UAI competitions demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution therefore concerns both the estimate itself and useful uncertainty bounds during ongoing computation.
neurips-2017-dynamic-importance-sampling.tldr: Dynamic importance sampling combines search and sampling to produce unbiased partition-function estimates with useful finite-sample bounds throughout computation.

paragraphs: This paper revisits optimal experimental design by introducing a family of mathematical objectives with a geometric interpretation. The objectives use elementary symmetric polynomials to capture partial volumes. They provide a graded transition between A-optimal and D-optimal design, including both established models as special cases within the same framework.

The authors analyze the properties of these objectives and develop two approaches to computing designs: greedy algorithms and algorithms based on convex relaxation. The analysis supplies approximation guarantees for these methods. This matters because the new objectives are accompanied by procedures for finding designs and theoretical statements about the quality those procedures can achieve.

Empirical results support the authors’ claims and reveal a phenomenon involving the greedy algorithm, although the abstract does not characterize that phenomenon. The work also yields new theoretical results about elementary symmetric polynomials. Its broader contribution is a unified family of design criteria connecting familiar endpoints, together with algorithmic and mathematical tools for working with the intermediate choices.
neurips-2017-elementary-symmetric-polyno.tldr: Geometrically motivated polynomial objectives connect A-optimal and D-optimal experimental design and admit algorithms with approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: EX2 addresses exploration when reinforcement learning rewards are sparse. Novelty can guide an agent toward states it has not adequately explored, but many novelty methods require generating or predicting observations. Training those models can be difficult when observations are complex and high-dimensional, including raw images.

The paper instead learns discriminative exemplar models. These classifiers try to distinguish each visited state from the other states encountered during training. The intuition is that an unusual state should be easier to distinguish from the agent’s previous experience. The authors show that this discriminative procedure corresponds to an implicit form of density estimation, connecting classification-based novelty to how frequently states occur.

They combine this novelty mechanism with count-based exploration and obtain competitive results across several popular benchmarks. On challenging egocentric observations in vizDoom, they report state-of-the-art results. The significance is that exploration can use a density-related novelty signal learned entirely through discrimination, providing an alternative to explicitly modeling how observations are generated or predicting their contents.
neurips-2017-ex2-exploration-with-exempl.tldr: EX2 guides exploration using classifiers that identify distinctive states, linking discriminative novelty detection to implicit density estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies supervised domain adaptation when only a few labeled examples are available from the target domain. The goal is to learn a shared representation that makes the two domains difficult to distinguish while aligning their semantic content. With very little target data, achieving appropriate alignment and separation of semantic distributions becomes especially difficult.

The proposed framework uses adversarial learning with a redesigned discriminator. Instead of the typical binary discrimination task, the discriminator distinguishes four classes within a carefully constructed training scheme. This change supports the simultaneous objectives of confusing domain identity and preserving semantic alignment in the learned embedding.

The authors report that adaptation can be effective with extremely few labeled target examples, including one per category. Here, adaptation speed refers to the number of labeled target samples required. They compare the method extensively with state-of-the-art domain adaptation approaches in handwritten digit recognition and visual object recognition experiments. The findings support the possibility of effective supervised adaptation with sparse target labels, without making a universal one-example guarantee.
neurips-2017-few-shot-adversarial-domain.tldr: A four-class adversarial training scheme supports domain adaptation with very few labeled target examples, sometimes just one per category.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a linear neural network learns a linear transformation under mean-squared loss. Its focus is the loss function’s critical points, where first-order changes provide no direction of improvement. The authors investigate their existence and optimality properties, with particular attention to how robust these points are when a small amount of regularization is introduced.

They formulate the problem using optimal control and derive backpropagation with weight decay through Hamilton’s formulation of that framework. This provides a common mathematical description of the learning procedure and the critical points it encounters. The resulting characterization expresses all critical points through solutions of a nonlinear matrix-valued characteristic equation.

The authors then use analytical and numerical tools from bifurcation theory to compute critical points from that equation. This makes the effects of regularization accessible through a structured mathematical problem. The contribution is a complete characterization within the proposed formulation and a way to investigate those solutions, rather than a blanket claim that regularization makes every critical point optimal.
neurips-2017-how-regularization-affects-.tldr: An optimal-control formulation characterizes critical points of regularized linear networks through a nonlinear matrix equation.

paragraphs: This paper transfers representations learned during machine translation to other language tasks. Its starting observation is that language models commonly initialize only their lowest layer with pretrained word vectors, whereas vision systems have benefited from transferring multiple pretrained layers. The authors investigate whether a deeper language encoder can likewise provide reusable information.

They take a deep LSTM encoder from an attentional sequence-to-sequence translation model and use it to produce contextualized word vectors, called CoVe. These vectors represent words in relation to their surrounding text. Adding them supplies downstream models with representations learned through the supervised translation task, alongside their existing word and character vectors.

Across sentiment analysis, question classification, entailment, and question answering, adding CoVe improves performance over using only unsupervised word and character representations. For fine-grained sentiment analysis and entailment, the additions bring the authors’ baseline models to state-of-the-art performance. The findings show that translation-trained context representations can transfer across a variety of language tasks, with the strongest stated result applying to those two task settings.
neurips-2017-learned-in-translation-cont.tldr: CoVe transfers a translation-trained LSTM encoder’s contextual word representations to improve several downstream language tasks.

paragraphs: This paper proposes training multiclass classifiers with complementary labels: annotations that identify a class an example does not belong to. Such labels could be easier to collect because annotators need not select the correct answer from a long list. Each annotation supplies less information than an ordinary label, so learning requires a method that accounts for this different form of supervision.

The authors show that complementary labels alone can produce an unbiased estimator of classification risk if the loss function satisfies a particular symmetry condition. That condition is part of the result: the claim does not cover arbitrary losses. They also derive estimation error bounds and prove that the method achieves the optimal parametric convergence rate.

The framework can combine complementary labels with ordinary labeled data, allowing both annotation types to contribute to learning. Experiments demonstrate the proposed methods’ usefulness. The central finding is that ruling out classes can support principled classification learning, including theoretical error guarantees under the stated loss condition, rather than serving only as an informal hint.
neurips-2017-learning-from-complementary.tldr: Complementary labels can support unbiased classification-risk estimation and optimal parametric convergence when the loss satisfies a specified symmetry condition.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression when training labels specify intervals of possible outcomes rather than exact numerical values. Such data arise in settings involving censored measurements, including genomics and medicine. The learner must still produce a real-valued prediction, but its training procedure needs to work with the partial information provided by each interval.

The authors investigate nonlinear tree models for this task, where most existing approaches use linear models. They propose a margin-based discriminative objective for learning the tree and give a dynamic programming algorithm that computes the optimal solution in log-linear time. This combines a nonlinear prediction model with an optimization procedure that has a stated efficiency guarantee.

On a benchmark containing several datasets, the method achieves state-of-the-art speed and prediction accuracy empirically. The result supports trees as a practical approach to interval-valued supervision, with both computational and predictive benefits in the reported evaluation. The algorithm’s optimality concerns the optimization problem it solves; the accuracy finding comes from the benchmark experiments.
neurips-2017-maximum-margin-interval-tre.tldr: Maximum Margin Interval Trees learn nonlinear regression models from interval-valued labels using an efficient dynamic programming algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper considers two agents making sequential decisions with the same reward function but different beliefs about how the world changes. Their disagreement concerns transition probabilities in an underlying Markovian model. Shared goals therefore do not automatically produce effective joint behavior, because the agents may expect different consequences from the same actions.

The proposed multi-view decision process captures this situation. An agent with the correct world model can commit to a particular policy, using that commitment to steer the other agent’s behavior and seek higher shared utility. The authors formally analyze the positive effects of such steering policies and develop an algorithm for computing an achievable joint policy.

Experiments show that the computed policy can produce a large utility increase when the agents’ models diverge. This highlights policy commitment as a way for an informed helper to improve cooperation despite differences in predictive beliefs. The setting specifically assumes common rewards and an agent with the correct model; the reported improvement is a demonstrated possibility within this framework.
neurips-2017-multi-view-decision-process.tldr: An agent with the correct world model can use policy commitment to improve shared utility when a cooperating agent holds different transition beliefs.

paragraphs: Tensor train decomposition offers a compact representation of higher-order tensors, which organize data across multiple dimensions. This paper addresses two obstacles to using that representation in machine learning: insufficient statistical theory and a lack of scalable algorithms. Compact storage is valuable, but practical learning also needs an understanding of reconstruction error and an efficient computation method.

The authors introduce a convex relaxation of the tensor train decomposition problem. For tensor completion, where the aim is to recover a tensor from partial observations, they derive an error bound. They also develop a randomized optimization method whose time complexity is described as being as efficient as its space complexity, connecting computational scalability to the representation’s storage advantage.

Experiments numerically confirm the derived bounds and demonstrate the method on a real higher-order tensor. These findings supply both theoretical and empirical support for the proposed approach. The paper’s contribution is the combination of a statistically analyzed relaxation and scalable optimization, addressing separate requirements for making tensor train methods useful in learning problems.
neurips-2017-on-tensor-train-rank-minimi.tldr: A convex relaxation and randomized optimizer give tensor train learning statistical error bounds and scalable computation.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bidder who repeatedly allocates a budget among bids for multiple goods. The aim is to maximize total payoff over T periods, so each allocation is part of an ongoing learning problem. The authors seek a strategy that is computationally practical and has a provable bound on the payoff lost through learning.

Their algorithm, dynamic programming on discrete set, or DPDS, draws inspiration from dynamic programming for the knapsack problem. It runs in polynomial time and achieves regret of order O(sqrt(T log T)). The authors also prove an Omega(sqrt(T)) regret lower bound for any strategy. Together, these results place DPDS within a factor of sqrt(log T) of the optimal regret order.

The empirical evaluation uses historical New York wholesale electricity market data for virtual trading. DPDS consistently outperforms the benchmark heuristics derived from machine learning and online learning approaches. Thus, the paper combines a near-order-optimal theoretical result with evidence of effective bidding in the evaluated market setting, while retaining the logarithmic gap in its regret guarantee.
neurips-2017-online-learning-of-optimal-.tldr: DPDS learns budget allocations for repeated auctions in polynomial time with regret within a square-root-logarithmic factor of the optimal order.

paragraphs: This paper studies online linear optimization when the learner receives a hint before choosing its action each round. The hint is a vector weakly correlated with that round’s loss vector. The question is how much this limited advance information can help, and the answer depends on the geometry of the set of available actions.

When the feasible set is strongly convex, the authors show that hints can support regret of O(log T) over T rounds. For a q-uniformly convex set with q between 2 and 3, they establish regret of o(sqrt(T)), meaning growth strictly slower than the square-root scale. Both results require the corresponding geometric conditions on feasible actions.

For polyhedral feasible sets, the authors instead establish regret lower bounds of Omega(sqrt(T)). This contrast makes the set’s shape central to the value of weak predictive information. The contribution is a conditional account of when hints can yield stronger guarantees, together with lower bounds showing that the same improvement cannot be promised across all action-set geometries.
neurips-2017-online-learning-with-a-hint.tldr: Weakly informative hints can sharply reduce online-learning regret when the feasible action set has suitable curvature.

paragraphs: This paper uses deep learning to select mathematical statements that are relevant to proving a conjecture. Premise selection is a filtering problem: the system must recognize which available statements are useful for the proof under consideration. The authors focus on representing logical formulas in a way that exposes their structure to a learned model.

They encode higher-order logic formulas as graphs that remain unchanged under variable renaming while preserving syntactic and semantic information. This means that changing variable names does not change the representation of the formula’s content. A new graph embedding method then converts each graph into a vector while retaining information about the ordering of edges.

These representation choices let the model handle naming invariance without discarding structural distinctions carried by the formula. On the HolStep dataset, the approach raises classification accuracy from 83% to 90.3%, achieving state-of-the-art results. The reported finding concerns the premise-selection classification task and demonstrates the effectiveness of this structure-preserving graph representation in that evaluation.
neurips-2017-premise-selection-for-theor.tldr: Structure-preserving graph embeddings improve premise-selection accuracy on HolStep from 83% to 90.3%.

paragraphs: This paper adapts batch Bayesian optimization to experiments where some settings are expensive or time-consuming to change. Within a recommended batch, those settings must remain fixed, while other control variables can vary. The optimization problem therefore needs to account for how experiments are physically carried out when choosing a group of recommendations.

The authors formalize this as process-constrained batch Bayesian optimization and propose two algorithms. The simpler pc-BO(basic) lacks a convergence guarantee. The slightly more complex pc-BO(nested) permits convergence analysis, and the authors prove sublinear regret for it. That guarantee concerns the nested method and does not automatically extend to the basic version.

They demonstrate both algorithms on benchmark functions, SVM hyperparameter tuning, alloy heat-treatment optimization for target hardness, and short polymer fibre production. These applications illustrate the relevance of coordinating fixed and adjustable settings across a batch. The contribution combines a formulation reflecting experimental constraints with practical algorithms, including one supported by a theoretical statement about its learning performance over time.
neurips-2017-process-constrained-batch-b.tldr: Two batch Bayesian optimization algorithms handle settings that must remain fixed within each batch, with sublinear regret proved for the nested variant.

paragraphs: This paper examines why injecting noise into hidden units can help neural networks generalize, and how that training procedure can be improved. Dropout is a motivating example. The authors focus on the tension between fitting the true data distribution and using regularization to prevent overfitting, seeking an objective-based explanation of noise’s role.

They interpret conventional noise-injection training as optimizing a lower bound on the true objective. This viewpoint identifies a gap between the objective being optimized during noisy training and the underlying target. The proposed technique uses multiple noise samples for each training example within a stochastic gradient descent iteration to obtain a tighter lower bound.

The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this idea in several computer vision applications. The contribution connects an explanation of existing noise regularization to a specific change in training: evaluating multiple noise realizations for the same example. Its theoretical motivation is the tighter bound, while the application results provide empirical support for the usefulness of that modification.
neurips-2017-regularizing-deep-neural-ne.tldr: Viewing noise regularization as lower-bound optimization motivates using multiple noise samples per example to tighten the training objective.

paragraphs: This paper revises the Hidden Parameter Markov Decision Process, a framework for representing families of related tasks. The framework uses low-dimensional latent embeddings to capture task variation. Those hidden parameters provide a compact way to describe differences among tasks while treating them as members of a shared modeling problem.

The new formulation correctly models joint uncertainty in the latent parameters and the state space. This concerns uncertainty about the task’s hidden characteristics together with uncertainty associated with its states. Treating these jointly is a central modeling change, because the framework needs to represent both within its account of related decision-making tasks.

The authors also replace the original Gaussian process model with a Bayesian neural network to enable more scalable inference. The abstract attributes an expanded application scope to these changes, including higher-dimensional problems and more complex dynamics. The contribution therefore combines a revision to uncertainty modeling with a computationally more scalable model, broadening the kinds of related-task families that the HiP-MDP framework can address.
neurips-2017-robust-and-efficient-transf.tldr: A revised HiP-MDP models joint task-and-state uncertainty and uses a Bayesian neural network for more scalable inference.

paragraphs: This paper connects a semisupervised clustering problem to data compression. In the clustering setting, a learner submits a collection of simple queries in parallel and receives binary answers that may contain errors. Each query involves at most two elements, or a fixed constant number of elements. The learner must recover all class labels from these answers using as few queries as possible.

The authors prove that this setting is equivalent to locally encodable source coding, where each compressed bit depends on only a few input bits. This equivalence turns constraints on local query information into a compression problem. It allows them to derive lower bounds on the number of queries needed in a variety of scenarios.

They also establish fundamental limitations of pairwise queries asking whether two elements share a cluster. As an alternative, they propose pairwise AND queries and prove that these perform better in many situations. The result shows that query design matters alongside query count, with the advantage established for multiple settings rather than asserted universally.
neurips-2017-semisupervised-clustering-a.tldr: An equivalence between clustering queries and local source coding yields query lower bounds and proves advantages for pairwise AND queries in many settings.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the theory of training neural networks with coarsely quantized weights. Direct low-precision training matters for embedded systems with limited computation, memory, and power. The authors distinguish this goal from the common workflow of training a full-precision model on powerful hardware and then deriving a low-precision version for inference.

They first examine accuracy guarantees under convexity assumptions. These assumptions define the setting of that part of the analysis and should not be carried over automatically to general neural-network training. The paper then studies algorithm behavior on nonconvex problems, where the role of higher-precision representations becomes central.

The authors show that training methods using high-precision representations have an important greedy search phase that purely quantized methods lack. This difference provides an explanation for the difficulty of training with low-precision arithmetic. The contribution moves beyond empirical comparisons by identifying an algorithmic behavior associated with higher precision and relating it to the challenges of direct quantized learning.
neurips-2017-training-quantized-nets-a-d.tldr: Theoretical analysis links the difficulty of purely quantized training to a greedy search phase available to methods retaining high-precision representations.

paragraphs: This paper extends a transformation technique for graphical models from binary pairwise models to models with higher-order potentials. Uprooting and rerooting produce related models in an equivalence class, where inference results for one can yield results for the others. This creates an opportunity to work with a representation on which inference or relevant bounds are easier or more accurate.

The authors introduce methods that support these transformations for higher-order interactions and develop theoretical insights into their behavior. One result identifies the triplet-consistent polytope, TRI, as uniquely possessing the property termed universally rooted. This is a specific structural characterization within the theory accompanying the extended transformation methods.

Experiments show that rerooting can significantly improve the accuracy of inference methods for higher-order models at negligible computational cost. The practical significance is that changing the model’s representation can improve an inference procedure while retaining access to results for the related models. The reported improvement is empirical and expressed as a capability, rather than a guarantee for every model and inference method.
neurips-2017-uprooting-and-rerooting-hig.tldr: Rerooting extends to higher-order graphical models and can substantially improve inference accuracy at negligible computational cost.

paragraphs: This paper models the sequence of eye movements through a dynamic scene using a principle inspired by physical mechanics. It proposes that attentional scanpaths can emerge from foundational laws expressed through a generalized least-action framework. The aim is to derive movement trajectories from a mathematical description of visual attention.

The model’s potential energy represents visual details and peripheral features, while its kinetic energy follows the classical mechanics interpretation. Its Lagrangian also includes a brightness-invariance term that substantially shapes the resulting scanpaths. The authors derive differential equations for attention by finding stationary points of the generalized action, turning the proposed principle into equations governing movement.

They additionally provide an algorithm for estimating the model’s parameters and report experiments validating it on saliency detection tasks. These steps connect the mathematical formulation to an estimable computational model and an empirical evaluation. The findings support the proposed approach in those tasks; the mechanics-inspired construction is a modeling principle, rather than an established universal law of human eye movement.
neurips-2017-variational-laws-of-visual-.tldr: A generalized least-action model derives visual-attention trajectories from image features, movement energy, and brightness invariance.

paragraphs: YASS addresses spike sorting for dense multi-electrode recordings, where signals from neurons appear across many electrodes. Its central strategy is to learn from clean events first and return later to difficult events. A neural-network detector and outlier triaging initially set aside noisy waveforms and collisions caused by two neurons firing synchronously.

The clean waveforms are clustered to infer neural spike templates using a nonparametric Bayesian approach. A coreset reduces the data handled during clustering, and efficient inference in a Dirichlet process mixture model improves scalability. Matching-pursuit deconvolution then recovers the waveforms that were temporarily excluded, so triaging is an intermediate step rather than permanent rejection.

The pipeline improves accuracy and stability over the state of the art on real and biophysically realistic simulated recordings. For a 500-electrode dataset, template learning and clustering run faster than real time, largely on one CPU core. That speed statement applies specifically to those stages. The results support separating clean-template discovery from subsequent recovery of more difficult events.
neurips-2017-yass-yet-another-spike-sort.tldr: YASS learns spike templates from clean events before recovering difficult waveforms, improving sorting accuracy, stability, and scalability.
